output: A road that PAYS voids the greedy license — Dijkstra locks the wrong answer
Bellman-Ford: one hop-budget layer per round — each solved exactly once
The spare round is a negative-cycle detector

props.text:
Shortest path, S to A?
10 — obviously
…right?

beats.narration_text: Here's a graph. Six places, eight roads, and one question: shortest route from S to A. There's a road that goes straight there. Ten. Any sensible algorithm grabs it, locks it, moves on. Dijkstra — the fast one, the famous one — does exactly that. Locked. Ten. And it is wrong. Not broken — misapplied. Dijkstra comes with a license printed on the box: every road must cost something. This graph has a road that pays. The license is void, and the algorithm has no way to notice.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE INSTANCE 1 · Graph runs the greedy failure; non-negative license is stamped VOID by −4.

beats.narration_text: So here's an algorithm that asks a more careful question. Not ‘how far is A?’ — but ‘how far is A if I'm allowed at most one hop? At most two?’ Round one answers every one-hop question: A ten, E eight. Round two, every two-hop question: D nine, C twelve. Each answer is final the moment it's written — for its question.

beats.narration_text: Round three. Look at D — nine. And that edge from D to A weighs minus four. A's guess says ten. Before I run it: what happens to A? Commit to an answer. Nine minus four. Five. The confident ten just lost to a detour through a road that pays you.

beats.narration_text: And the corrections cascade. C rides the new path down to eight. B: twelve becomes ten becomes six becomes — round five — five. Watch what's happening: each round, the truth reaches one hop further.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE TRANSFORM · Same cells morph through rounds 3–5; final vector is 0,5,5,8,9,8.

beats.narration_text: It looks like the algorithm keeps changing its mind. It never does. Lay the rounds out as their own rows and watch: every cell is written once and never touched again. ‘Distance to A’ was six different questions — at most zero hops, one, two — each solved exactly once from the row above. That discipline has a name: dynamic programming. Not saving answers for later — solving each subproblem once, and never, ever re-solving it. The table that seemed to flicker? Six rows sharing one line of storage. And notice what made the whole scheme legal — two things this problem has that not every problem does. The questions come in an order: smaller hop-budgets before bigger ones. And answers are permanent: letting yourself take more hops can never change what the best three-hop route was. No ordering, no DP. No permanence, nothing safe to store. Five vertices minus one rounds, and no shortest path needs more. The edge-by-edge step finally deserves its name: relaxation.

beats.narration_text: One catch — and it is the whole reason the round count matters. A route that never repeats a node can use at most five edges — six nodes, five hops. And our invariant says: after five rounds, every route like that is already priced. Now make B to A minus one. The lap A, C, B, back to A costs two, minus two, minus one: minus one per lap. Round six finds a shorter path. But how? Any longer route must revisit some node. Cut that loop out, and what remains is a no-repeat route — already priced. So the only thing the lap could have added is its own total. If the route got cheaper, that total is negative. A negative cycle — and shortest stops meaning anything, because every extra lap pays. The sixth round isn't waste. It's the proof, running as a smoke detector.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE INSTANCE 3 / TRACE 2 · D→A changes −4→−9; round six changes again; cycle labeled NEGATIVE.

beats.narration_text: So: S to A. Not the road that says ten. Eight, plus one, minus four. Five. The greedy answer wasn't unlucky — the graph broke the rule Dijkstra's correctness depends on. That's the real first question for any algorithm — not ‘what are the steps?’ but ‘what must be true of my problem for those steps to be legal?’ Dijkstra asks for non-negative roads. Bellman-Ford asks only for ordered questions and answers that stay answered.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE PAYOFF · Same graph returns; 10 shatters and S→E→D→A is labeled 8+1−4=5.

beats.narration_text: The verdict. Dijkstra isn't broken — it was unlicensed: one road that pays voided it. Bellman-Ford changes the question: shortest path using at most k hops — six questions, not one. Ordered questions, permanent answers, each layer solved exactly once. That is dynamic programming. And the spare sixth round is the proof, running as a smoke detector.

artifactLines: Dijkstra's license: every weight ≥ 0 — this graph voided it (edge −4)
The real question: shortest using ≤ k hops — six questions, not one
Ordering + permanence: each (v, k) solved exactly once, never re-solved
S→A = 5 via S→E→D→A — the road marked 10 was never shortest
Round 6 improving ⇒ a repeated node ⇒ a loop that pays: negative cycle
